newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ingwe yr shr seen up,coal prices to dim '98.
newsitem.headline: Ingwe yr shr seen up,coal prices to dim '98.

text.p: South African coal producer Ingwe Coal Corp Ltd is expected to post good gains in earnings this year, but a strain on world coal prices looks set to tame its profits in 1998, analysts said on Thursday.

A Reuters consensus poll forecast Ingwe's earnings per share rising by 41 percent to 329 cents from a previous 234 cents when the firm reports its results for the year to June 1997 on Monday. The range was between 310-350 cents.
The dividend was seen up 43 percent to 157 cents from a range of 145 to 175 cents.
Analysts said a weaker rand in the fourth quarter of last year had boosted Ingwe's exports to the European market which accounts for about 55 percent of its export sales.

They said there had also been no operational glitches at its collieries after the firm lost nearly a million tonnes of production from flooding at its mines in the Mpumalanga Province in March last year.
Ingwe put the quantifiable effect of the floods in excess of 114 million rand.

"It's a good year, a very good year with earnings growth up...In the first half of their financial year, June to December last year, the rand was very weak against the dollar and also in that period coal prices were also a lot firmer...," Mike Byrne of stockbroking firm Edey Rogers & Co told Reuters.
"I think they've also had a better six months operationally, if you remember the floods in their mines in March last year."
Analysts said while Ingwe's results were expected to be better, they held no value for the future as world coal prices were set to tumble on increased over-capacity in South East Asia.

They said to add to the gloom of Ingwe's future earnings growth prospects, a decline in coal demand was expected as Europe continued to shift to more environmentally-friendly energy sources such as gas.

"Every year people are using less and less coal in Europe -- there's a number of reasons for that -- in coal-fired power stations they've upgraded technology and they've become more efficient, the second thing is that you've got gas now that the Cold War is over..." Byrne said.
"The results coming out are all history. Next year they are down, they are going to be under pressure if you look at what's happening now," said another analyst who declined to be identified.
"Spot prices have tumbled and prices are going to remain under pressure. It's not a particularly brave market at this stage," the analyst said.

Despite the dimmed outlook for coal prices, Europe's moves towards European economic and monetary union (EMU) could create an import gap as governments cut subsidies to state-funded coal enterprises in order to comply with the Maastricht Treaty, Byrne said.

"You are going to see mines closing in Europe. So while demand is pretty flat, supply within Europe is very, very negative. That creates a bigger import gap for people like Ingwe and especially Colombian producers to step in," he said.
Ingwe exports nearly 60 percent of its total production.
